reply_verbatim.reasons: Style 1 keeps the kingdom crimson on every citizen's torso, so it reads from above. The three roles separate clearly: the farmer has a straw hat and hoe, the soldier a grey helmet with a crest and pennant spear, and the ruler a crown, ermine collar and gold-trimmed robe. It stays well under budget at 886/924/1080 triangles, which leaves room for more variants (hats, tabards, tools). Its faceted low-poly shapes sit comfortably beside the cottage, and its proportions match the chunky Roblox look. Style 3 is close, but it is heavier (1164 to 1444 triangles) and gives up some of the colour read, so Style 1 is the safer foundation.
pick_defects: The faces are tiny and the expressions are unconvincing in the portrait: the farmer's mouth and the soldier's eyes are hard to read, and the ruler looks glum.

In the aerial view the soldier's grey helmet and arms and the ruler's white sleeves wash out the crimson, so the figures look pale and similar. The ruler's body reads as roughly the same height and shape as the soldier's.
The farmer's cream apron and grey sleeves read as muddy and a little dull at 40 studs. The ruler's collar and shoulder blobs are chunky and lumpy, and the hoe head is a plain white block.

Style 2: The kingdom colour is mostly lost: the soldier and ruler wear grey armour, so crimson shows only on the hat or helmet and crest. From the aerial view the soldier and ruler look nearly identical grey figures.

The finer detail (a hair-textured farmer, a spiky helmet, painted limbs) turns to noise at 40 studs. It also costs the most, with the ruler at 1438 against a 1500 cap, and the glossy, painterly look clashes with the flat cottage.
Style 3: The triangle counts are higher than Style 1 for little visible gain (farmer 1164, ruler 1444), and the faces are flat with stern, heavy brows.
The ruler and soldier bodies are very similar in shape and colour at distance, and the dark brown and olive legs make the figures look muddy next to Style 1's cleaner colours.
